t.4.27.1: Then Rāma, having slain Vālin and consecrated Sugrīva, while dwelling on the ridge of Mālyavant, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
t.4.27.2: This is that time which has now arrived, the season of the coming of the waters. Behold the sky, covered with clouds that resemble mountains.
t.4.27.3: Having drunk the waters of the oceans through the rays of the sun, the sky now gives birth to the life-giving elixir, the embryo it has carried for nine months.
t.4.27.4: Now one could climb up into the sky by the rows of clouds as by flights of steps, and adorn the sun with garlands of kuṭaja and arjuna flowers.
t.4.27.6: The sky, its sighs the gentle breeze, tinted with the sandalwood paste of twilight, its clouds pale white, shines like one tormented by love.
t.4.27.5: With smooth cloud-cloths for coverings, coppery with the rising glow of twilight and paler at their edges, the sky looks as though its wounds had been bandaged.
t.4.27.8: Released from the bellies of the clouds, pleasantly cool with the touch of white water-lilies and fragrant with ketakī blossoms, the winds can be drunk in with cupped hands.
t.4.27.7: This earth, worn out by the heat and now drenched with fresh rain, releases vapour, like Sītā shedding tears, burning with grief.
t.4.27.9: This mountain, its arjuna trees in full bloom and perfumed by ketaka flowers, is being bathed by torrents of rain, like Sugrīva, his enemy subdued, being anointed with streams of consecrating water.
t.4.27.10: Wearing the clouds as black antelope-skins and the streams of rain as sacred threads, their caves filled with the wind, the mountains seem like students who have begun their Vedic recitation.
t.4.27.11: Struck by flashes of lightning as though by golden whips, the sky, with the roar of thunder rumbling deep within it, seems to groan as if in pain.
t.4.27.12: The lightning, clinging to the dark-blue cloud and flashing, appears to me like the wretched Vaidehī struggling in the lap of Rāvaṇa.
t.4.27.13: Here are those very quarters, so pleasing to the lovelorn, now blocked from view, as though smeared over by the clouds, their planets and moon lost to sight.
t.4.27.14: Look, Saumitri, at the kuṭaja trees in blossom here and there on the mountain slopes, choked as if with tears and eager for the coming of the rains; they stand there kindling desire in me, who am overwhelmed by grief.
t.4.27.16: Now the cakravāka birds, longing to dwell at Mānasa, have set out together with their mates, while on the roads battered by the incessant rainwater, vehicles no longer travel.
t.4.27.15: The dust has settled, today the wind is cool, and the spreading torments of the hot season have subsided. The marches of the lords of the earth have come to a halt, and men who are abroad return to their own lands.
t.4.27.17: The sky, strewn with scattered clouds, shines bright in some places and dark in others, and here and there it is hemmed in by mountains, looking like the form of a great ocean grown calm.
t.4.27.19: The jambu fruit, full of juice and dark like a bee, is eaten to one's heart's content; and the ripe mango fruit of many colours, shaken by the wind, falls to the ground.
t.4.27.18: The mountain streams swiftly carry their fresh water, mingled with sarja and kadamba blossoms and reddened like copper by the mountain minerals, while the cries of peacocks follow along after it.
t.4.27.20: With lightning for their banners and garlands of cranes, resembling in form the peaks of the lord of mountains, the clouds thunder with loud-rising roars, like maddened lordly elephants standing in battle.
t.4.27.21: The row of cranes, longing for the clouds, flying about together in delight, shines like a long garland of choice white lotuses, tossed by the wind, strung for the sky.
t.4.27.22: Sleep slowly approaches Keśava, the river swiftly approaches the ocean, the joyful crane approaches the cloud, and the beloved woman, full of desire, approaches her dear one.
t.4.27.23: The forest borders have come alive with peacocks dancing gracefully; the kadamba trees have come forth with branches laden with kadamba blossoms; the bulls have grown ardent for the cows with a desire matching theirs; and the earth has become lovely with crops and woodlands.
t.4.27.25: Thrilled at catching the fragrance of the ketaka flowers, the lordly elephants, joyful amid the forest waterfalls and stirred by the roar of the cascading torrents, trumpet in their rut together with the peacocks.
t.4.27.24: The rivers flow, the clouds pour rain, the rutting elephants trumpet, the forest tracts shine, those parted from their beloveds brood, the peacocks dance, and the monkeys take heart.
t.4.27.27: The branches of the jambu trees shine forth with their abundant fruits, full of rich juice and resembling heaps of charcoal dust, as though they were being settled upon by swarms of bees.
t.4.27.26: Battered by the falling torrents of rain and hanging from the branches of the kadamba trees, the six-footed bees slowly shed the intoxication they had gained in a moment, steeped deep in the nectar of flowers.
t.4.27.28: The forms of the clouds, adorned with banners of lightning and sending forth deep and mighty roars, shine like those of elephants eager for battle.
t.4.27.29: A rutting lord of elephants, following his path and roaming through the mountain forests, had set out, but on hearing the roar of the clouds he turned back, eager for battle and suspecting a rival elephant.
t.4.27.30: Thirsty birds with discoloured plumage joyfully drink the water given by the lord of the gods, which falls pure and spotless like pearls and clings to the cups of leaves.
t.4.27.31: Dark clouds brimming with fresh water, clinging to dark clouds, shine forth like mountains scorched by forest fire, firmly rooted upon mountains scorched by forest fire.
t.4.27.33: The marches of kings have come to an end, and the army turns back home; hostilities, and the roads as well, have been leveled by the rains.
t.4.27.32: The lordly elephants are in rut, the lordly bulls rejoice, and the lords of beasts rest more deeply in the forests; the lordly mountains are lovely, the lords of serpents lie hidden and still, and the lord of the gods sports with the rain-bearing clouds.
t.4.27.34: In the month of Prauṣṭhapada, this time for study has arrived for the brāhmaṇas who wish to recite the Veda, the singers of the Sāman.
t.4.27.35: Surely Bharata, lord of Kosala, having ceased from his undertakings and gathered in his stores, has now entered upon the Āṣāḍhī observance.
t.4.27.36: Surely the current of the swelling Sarayū is now surging, like the roar that would rise from Ayodhyā on seeing me coming home.
t.4.27.37: These rains abound in fine qualities, and Sugrīva, his enemy conquered, enjoys happiness together with his wife, established in his great kingdom.
t.4.27.38: But I, Lakṣmaṇa, whose wife has been carried off and who have fallen from a great kingdom, am sinking down like a river bank that has been soaked through.
t.4.27.39: My grief is vast, the rains make the ways exceedingly hard to travel, and Rāvaṇa is a mighty enemy; it all seems boundless to me.
t.4.27.41: Moreover, I do not wish to press the monkey, who has suffered greatly and has only after a long time been reunited with his wife, merely because my own task weighs more heavily on me.
t.4.27.42: For Sugrīva himself, having rested and knowing that the time has come, will recognize the help he has received; of this there is no doubt.
t.4.27.40: Seeing that this is no season for marching, and that the roads are exceedingly hard to travel, and with Sugrīva bowed before me in submission, I said nothing at all.
t.4.27.43: Therefore, O you of auspicious marks, I remain here biding my time, waiting for Sugrīva's favour and for the rivers to grow calm and clear.
t.4.27.44: For a hero who has received a favour is bound to repay it; the ungrateful man who makes no return strikes at the hearts of the noble-spirited.
t.4.27.45: Then Lakṣmaṇa, thus addressed, collected his mind and, with palms joined, honored that speech. He spoke to Rāma, whose appearance was most delightful, revealing his own auspicious view.
t.4.27.46: O lord of men, the lord of the monkeys will before long accomplish all this that you desire, just as it was promised. Awaiting the autumn and steadfast in your resolve to subdue the enemy, may you bear with this downpour of rain.
